The identification of potential hazards includes a detailed explanation of their origin, the possible consequences, and the management measures that can be implemented to mitigate or eliminate the associated risks. 2. Operators of small water systems serving fewer than 50 people or providing less than 10 cubic meters of water per day can utilize either a web-based tool or a simplified checklist developed by the Finnish Environment Institute to assist in hazard identification and risk mitigation. 3. Well owners who identify issues through risk assessments, water testing, or other means are eligible for grants under the Rural Water Programme to support improvement works. These grants are administered by local authorities (county councils) and can be used for activities such as constructing a pump house, installing treatment systems, or drilling a new well. Payments of up to €5000 are made after the completion and inspection of the work, provided the water supply meets quality and quantity standards. 4. In Vanuatu, community water suppliers are required to implement drinking-water safety and security plans under the Water Supply (Amendment) Act of 2016, the Water Resource Management (Amendment) Act of 2016, and the National Drinking Water Quality Standards of 2019. While routine operations and low-cost improvements are expected to be managed by the community, technical and financial assistance is available for more complex needs through the government’s Capital Assistance Programme. Requests for funding are reviewed and prioritized by provincial advisory committees and forwarded to the Department of Water Resources for further planning and budgeting. 5. In Cambodia, water safety planning is being used to strengthen the climate resilience of rural drinking-water supplies. Climate change, recognized as a critical threat, has led to increased droughts and floods, impacting water availability and quality. The Government of Cambodia aims to provide 100% of the rural population with improved water supplies by 2025, as outlined in the National Strategy for Rural Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene 2011–2025. Teuk Saat 1001, a local NGO, operates water treatment kiosks staffed by trained entrepreneurs and continues to develop preparedness strategies, such as connecting kiosks to alternative water sources and expanding laboratory testing to address emerging climate-related contaminants. 6. In Nigeria, the 2023 Guidelines for Rural Drinking Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance adopt a risk-based approach to prioritize higher-risk sites for more frequent surveillance. Local authorities are required to conduct sanitary inspections and water quality testing biannually during both rainy and dry seasons. Community-level monitoring is also conducted monthly using simple presence-absence tests with hydrogen sulfide vials, which serve as a screening mechanism to identify high-priority sites requiring additional surveillance. 7. In South Australia, the Safe Drinking Water Act 2011 mandates risk management plans to be audited or inspected annually or biennially, depending on the level of risk. Higher-risk water supplies, such as those serving vulnerable populations in regulated care or childcare facilities, are audited more frequently and by highly qualified practitioners. Follow-up inspections are conducted as needed to ensure deficiencies are addressed. 8. In England, local authorities regulate approximately 35,000 private water supplies, primarily in rural areas. The Private Water Supplies (England) Regulations 2016 require risk assessments and water quality monitoring, but resource limitations have led to incomplete compliance. To optimize public health benefits, higher-risk supplies serving larger populations or commercial activities are prioritized for site visits and up-to-date risk assessments. 9. In India, the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, aims to provide every rural household with a functional tap connection by 2024. The program integrates certified laboratory testing with community-led monitoring, empowering women in villages to conduct water quality tests using simple kits. A water quality management course and a knowledge exchange forum have been established to address gaps in surveillance capacity, and a Digital Academy is scaling these efforts nationwide. 10. In Iceland, health inspectors from Environmental Health Control oversee approximately 800 regulated drinking-water supplies, most of which are small and user-owned. To support their work, digitized sanitary inspection forms were developed starting in 2019, enabling inspectors to efficiently perform water quality sampling, risk management, and system maintenance across expansive areas.
